question.title: Machine Learning Definition
question.scenario: A data science team is building a model that analyzes historical sales data to predict future sales trends. The model automatically improves its predictions as more sales data becomes available without being explicitly reprogrammed.
question.question-text: What AI discipline is being applied in this scenario?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: What branch of AI is most associated with learning from data rather than following hand-coded rules?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Machine learning (B) is the correct answer because it is the AI discipline where algorithms learn patterns from historical data to make predictions, and improve automatically as more data becomes available. Expert systems (A) use hand-coded rules from domain experts and do not learn from data. Robotic process automation (C) automates repetitive tasks by mimicking user actions but does not learn or predict. Knowledge management (D) is about organizing and sharing information within an organization, not about data-driven prediction. The scenario's emphasis on learning from data and improving over time is the hallmark of machine learning.

ul.li: Machine learning is a subset of AI. The AI-900 exam tests the relationship hierarchy: AI is the parent discipline, ML is a subset of AI, and deep learning is a subset of ML that uses neural networks with multiple layers.

ML is distinct from traditional programming: in traditional programming you provide rules and data to get answers; in ML you provide data and answers to get rules (the model). This inversion is a core exam concept.
Azure Machine Learning is the primary Azure service for building custom ML models, supporting the full lifecycle from data preparation through model training, evaluation, and deployment as endpoints.
Expert systems were prominent in early AI (1970s-80s) and relied on manually curated knowledge bases with inference engines. They do not scale or adapt like ML approaches do.

question.title: Azure AI Vision Overview
question.scenario: A company wants to automatically extract information from images, including detecting objects, reading text in images, and generating captions. They need a pre-built AI service that doesn't require training custom models.
question.question-text: Which Azure service provides pre-built computer vision capabilities?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The team needs off-the-shelf image analysis — no custom training. Which Azure service offers pre-built vision APIs?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure AI Vision (D) is correct because it provides pre-built APIs for image analysis including object detection, OCR (reading text in images), image captioning, and more, all without requiring custom model training. Azure Machine Learning (A) is a platform for building custom models, not pre-built vision APIs. Azure Cognitive Search (B) is a search-as-a-service platform for indexing and querying content. Azure Bot Service (C) is for building conversational chatbots. The key requirement is "pre-built" and "doesn't require training custom models," which points to Azure AI Vision's ready-to-use APIs.

ul.li: Azure AI Vision (formerly Computer Vision service) offers these key capabilities: Image Analysis 4.0 (tagging, captioning, object detection, smart cropping), OCR (extracting printed and handwritten text), spatial analysis (people counting and movement tracking), and image retrieval (searching images by text or image queries).

Azure AI Vision vs. Custom Vision: AI Vision provides pre-built general-purpose models that work out of the box. Custom Vision lets you train specialized models for your specific domain using your own labeled images. For AI-900, if the scenario says "pre-built" or "no custom training," the answer is AI Vision. If it says "train a custom model" with domain-specific images, the answer is Custom Vision.

Azure AI Vision is accessed via REST APIs or client SDKs. You create a resource in Azure, get an endpoint and key, then send images to the API and receive JSON results with detected objects, tags, captions, and text. No ML expertise required.

Azure AI Vision is part of the broader Azure AI Services family (formerly Cognitive Services), which groups pre-built AI capabilities into vision, speech, language, and decision categories. Each category has multiple services accessible via API.

question.title: Video Analysis
question.scenario: A sports analytics company wants to analyze recorded game footage. They need to track player movements, detect key events like goals, and identify players throughout the video.
question.question-text: Which Azure service provides AI capabilities for analyzing video content?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The input is video, not still images. Which Azure service is purpose-built for extracting insights from video content?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure Video Indexer (C) is correct because it is specifically designed to extract deep insights from video content, including face detection and tracking, scene detection, object tracking, OCR in video, audio transcription, and key event identification. Azure AI Vision (A) analyzes individual images but is not designed for temporal video analysis with tracking and event detection across frames. Azure Custom Vision (B) trains custom image models but does not process video streams. Azure Stream Analytics (D) processes real-time data streams for IoT and telemetry, not video content analysis. Video Indexer combines multiple AI capabilities to provide comprehensive video understanding.

ul.li: Azure Video Indexer extracts a rich set of insights from video: face detection and identification, OCR (text on screen), audio transcription and translation, scene and shot detection, topic extraction, named entity recognition, sentiment analysis of spoken content, and visual content moderation.

Video Indexer produces a searchable, timestamped index of video content. This means you can search for when a specific person appears, when a topic is discussed, or when specific text is shown on screen. This transforms passive video archives into searchable knowledge bases.

Video Indexer vs. AI Vision: AI Vision can analyze individual video frames as images, but Video Indexer understands temporal relationships across frames (tracking, event detection, scene transitions). If the scenario requires understanding what happens over time in a video, Video Indexer is the answer.

Azure Stream Analytics is a common distractor because it also involves "streaming," but it processes structured data streams (IoT telemetry, event data), not video content. Stream Analytics uses SQL-like queries on data streams; Video Indexer uses AI models on media content.

question.title: Natural Language Processing Overview
question.scenario: A company wants to build an AI system that can understand and respond to customer emails, extract key information from support tickets, and automatically categorize incoming messages by topic.
question.question-text: What field of AI deals with enabling computers to understand and process human language?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario is entirely about understanding and processing written human language. Which broad AI field covers that?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Natural Language Processing or NLP (C) is correct because it is the AI field dedicated to enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language in both text and speech forms. Computer vision (A) processes images and video, not text. Robotics (B) deals with physical machines that interact with the physical world. Expert systems (D) use hand-coded rules from domain experts for decision-making but are not a field focused on language understanding. The scenario describes multiple NLP tasks: understanding emails (comprehension), extracting key information (information extraction), and categorizing messages (text classification).

ul.li: NLP encompasses many sub-tasks tested on AI-900: sentiment analysis (emotional tone), named entity recognition (identifying people, places, organizations), key phrase extraction (important terms), language detection (identifying which language), text classification (categorizing text), summarization (condensing text), translation (converting between languages), and question answering (finding answers in text).

On Azure, NLP capabilities are provided by several services: Azure AI Language (text analytics, entity recognition, sentiment, CLU), Azure AI Translator (language translation), Azure AI Speech (speech-to-text, text-to-speech), and Azure OpenAI Service (generative language capabilities). Know which service provides which NLP capability.

NLP has evolved significantly with transformer-based models. Traditional NLP used rule-based and statistical approaches. Modern NLP uses pre-trained language models (BERT, GPT) that understand context and semantics. Azure AI services use these modern approaches under the hood.

NLP and computer vision increasingly overlap in multimodal AI. For example, image captioning combines vision and language. Azure OpenAI's GPT-4 models accept both text and image inputs. However, for AI-900, these remain distinct workload categories.

question.title: Language Detection
question.scenario: A global customer service center receives messages in many different languages. Before routing messages to the appropriate language team, they need to automatically identify which language each message is written in.
question.question-text: What NLP capability identifies the language of input text?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Before the system can process a message, it must first figure out what language it's written in. Which NLP capability handles that first step?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Language detection (A) is correct because it identifies the language of input text, returning a language code (e.g., "en" for English, "fr" for French) along with a confidence score. Translation (B) converts text from one language to another but first requires knowing the source language, or it performs detection as an internal step. Sentiment analysis (C) determines emotional tone of text, not its language. Text classification (D) categorizes text into predefined topics or categories, not languages. Language detection is the specific capability for identifying what language text is written in, and it is typically the first step in a multilingual processing pipeline.

ul.li: Azure AI Language's language detection supports over 120 languages and scripts. It returns the detected language name, ISO 639-1 code (e.g., "en"), and a confidence score between 0 and 1. For ambiguous text, it may return "unknown" with a low confidence score.

Language detection is often the first step in a multi-step NLP pipeline. For example: detect language, then route to language-specific sentiment analysis, then translate to a common language for unified reporting. Azure AI Language can perform detection as a standalone call.

Azure AI Translator also includes automatic language detection as part of its translation API. When you send text for translation without specifying the source language, the translator auto-detects it. This is useful when detection and translation are needed together.

Edge cases for language detection include: mixed-language text (returns the dominant language), very short text (may have low confidence), and closely related languages (e.g., Bosnian, Croatian, Serbian share vocabulary). The exam tests awareness that short or ambiguous text may produce lower confidence results.

question.title: Large Language Models
question.scenario: A developer is working with an AI model trained on vast amounts of text data. The model can understand context, generate human-like text, answer questions, summarize documents, and write code based on natural language instructions.
question.question-text: What type of AI model has these broad language understanding and generation capabilities?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: This model handles many different language tasks from a single pre-trained foundation. What class of model is known for that versatility?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Large Language Model or LLM (A) is correct because LLMs are trained on massive text datasets and can perform a wide range of language tasks without task-specific training, including text generation, question answering, summarization, translation, and code writing. A regression model (B) predicts continuous numeric values for a single specific task. A classification model (C) predicts categories for a single specific task. A clustering model (D) groups similar data points. These traditional ML models are narrow and task-specific, while LLMs are general-purpose language models that handle many tasks through natural language prompting.

ul.li: LLMs are built on the Transformer architecture and trained using self-supervised learning on massive text corpora (billions to trillions of tokens). Examples include GPT-4, GPT-3.5, LLaMA, and PaLM. Azure OpenAI Service provides access to GPT models. The "large" in LLM refers to both the model size (billions of parameters) and the training data volume.

LLMs exhibit emergent capabilities that appear at scale: in-context learning (performing tasks from examples in the prompt), chain-of-thought reasoning (solving problems step by step), and instruction following (responding to natural language instructions). These capabilities are not explicitly trained; they emerge from scale.

LLMs use next-token prediction as their core mechanism: given a sequence of tokens, the model predicts the most likely next token. This simple objective, at sufficient scale, produces models that appear to understand and reason about language. Understanding this mechanism helps explain both LLM capabilities and limitations.

Key LLM limitations for the exam: they can hallucinate (generate plausible but false information), have a knowledge cutoff date (do not know about events after training), have context window limits (cannot process unlimited text), and may exhibit biases present in their training data.

question.title: Grounding with RAG
question.scenario: A company wants their generative AI to answer questions using their internal documentation. They implement a system that retrieves relevant documents from their knowledge base and includes that content in prompts to the language model.
question.question-text: What technique enhances AI responses by including retrieved information in prompts?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The system first searches a knowledge store, then feeds what it finds into the model's prompt. Which technique pairs document retrieval with AI generation?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation or RAG (C) is correct because it enhances generative AI responses by first retrieving relevant documents from an external knowledge source and then including that content in the prompt, grounding the model's responses in factual, up-to-date information. Fine-tuning (A) retrains the model on custom data to permanently alter its weights, not dynamically retrieving content at query time. Transfer learning (B) applies knowledge from one pre-trained model to a new task through additional training. Few-shot learning (D) provides examples in the prompt to guide the model's format and style but does not involve dynamic document retrieval. RAG uniquely combines search and generation at inference time.

ul.li: RAG works in three steps: (1) the user's question is used to search a knowledge base (using vector search, keyword search, or hybrid), (2) the most relevant documents are retrieved and added to the prompt as context, (3) the LLM generates a response grounded in the retrieved content. This process happens at query time, not during model training.

RAG solves key LLM limitations: hallucination (grounding responses in real documents reduces fabrication), knowledge cutoff (the knowledge base can contain current information), and domain specificity (the knowledge base contains your organization's proprietary content). It is the most practical approach for enterprise AI applications.

On Azure, RAG is typically implemented using Azure AI Search as the retrieval component and Azure OpenAI as the generation component. Azure AI Search indexes your documents and provides vector, semantic, and hybrid search. Azure OpenAI generates responses grounded in the search results. This is called the "Azure OpenAI on your data" pattern.

RAG vs. fine-tuning: RAG dynamically retrieves relevant information at query time without modifying the model. Fine-tuning permanently changes the model's weights by training on custom data. RAG is better for factual grounding with frequently updated content; fine-tuning is better for changing the model's style, tone, or domain-specific behavior.
